I'm not qualified to give advice, but I have a lot of experience and can share some insights I've collected along the way. 1. Keeping healthy is important. At 72, I still workout 4-5 times a week and though I can no longer run due to service related back injuries, I walk most mornings before dawn, I walk the dogs at dawn, and whenever possible, I use stairs instead of elevators or escalators. 2. Adventures in life are important, at least for me. I perhaps pushed the envelope more than most, but I never thought I was ever in real danger--well except for combat and free climbing. I think those very special memories add to a life and a sense of accomplishment. 3. I started late, but when I was a major in the Marines, I realized that military retirement is OK, but not sufficient to live comfortably, so I began investing 10% of my pay in mutual funds. The market goes up and down, but over the long haul it always goes up. Just because the market tanks occasionally, it's important not to panic and sell low. I would ride it out and kept investing because I was then buying stocks low and the market would go up over time and I'm make even more of those purchases. I'm thankful that I had the sense to plan for the long term as between my military retirement, SS, and my investments, I have a reasonably comfortable life in retirement. 4. I try to keep my mind active. I've always been very good at pattern analysis and finding solutions--which came in handy in combat. In fact, I think challenging the mind has been very important in my quality of life. I've done this in many different ways such as becoming a private pilot with commercial and instrument ratings. Flying is mentally challenging--especially on instruments at night when you have to think in three dimensions using only your instruments. I took up aerobatics for the adventure but it too was mentally challenging. SCUBA diving requires knowing what your limits are and constantly recalculating decompression times and depths before you ascend. I became a glider pilot just for the heck of it but it takes a lot of mental calculations to keep within range of the landing area using updrafts and you only have on chance at nailing the landing--there are no second chances in a glider. I took up sailing in the Hawaiian Islands and it too was challenging. There are dozens of things to consider such as wind, waves, currents, navigation, how much sail to put up, weather conditions, ocean temperatures (hypothermia considerations), but sky diving was just pure fun--nothing to think about except the altitude you open the chute. I've done much more, but you get the idea. Fun, adventure, and keeping mentally challenged. 5. I don't know what your profession is, but striking out on your own is difficult but it is also the most rewarding part of my life. I think I've had a rather none typical life. I served 21 years in the Marines as an infantry officer with 3 years in combat. During those years I was assigned a wide variety of jobs: platoon commander, company commander, instructor, logistician, intelligence officer, military attache at a US Embassy, and so on. But the job that I perhaps liked the least was the job that benefited me most after I retired from the Marine Corps.

At Headquarters Marine Corps, Wash DC, I was assigned as the projects officer to automate the Marine Corps' officer assignment system. The year was 1978, before the personal computer. To understand that the Marine Corps had just made the greatest mismatch of resource to requirements in Marine history. I only knew that NASA used computers, I had never seen a computer, I had no concept of an operating system, and I had no idea what a computer program was. In the early days of my Marine career, there was a philosophy that a Marine officer was qualified to do everything except fly a plane.

In order to understand what a computer was, I found that a store called Heathkit (later Radio Shack) sold parts that could be assembled into a primitive computer. Long story, but I bought several boxes of parts and a soldering iron and proceeded to build a computer in my basement. When I turned it on, one of the vacuum tubes exploded and sparks flew everywhere. Obviously, I did something wrong. So I built a second computer and this time the monitor had a small white line flashing in the upper left hand corner, but I had no idea what it was for. There was also a thin slot in the computer and I had no idea what that was for either. No matter what I did, I couldn't get it to do anything.

Then I learned I needed something called and operating system and so I bought the only one for sale at the time called CPM. I could now type letters and numbers but that was it.

Then I learned I needed something called a program and bought Pong which was mindless game with a ball bouncing around and I thought there is no way I'm going to automate the entire officer assignment system.

But I studied long hours and learned a great deal about computers. I learned to operate the main frame computer in the basement of Marine Headquarters. I taught myself how to program in FORTRAN as that was the main language used. There was no online programming in those days. I had to teach myself how up program using a card punch machine that produced one card for each line of code that were then kept in order in card decks and card decks were fed into a card reader that loaded the program into the main frame. But the Marine Corps wanted to use a new language for the computer printouts call "Natural" which was the forerunner to SQL.

I worked very long hours 6 days a week--some times 7 days. It took me a little over 3 years to complete the project. I had written over 500,000 lines of Natural code to produce all of the needed printouts. But I had the equivalent of a masters degree in computer science even though I didn't get a piece of paper to hang on the wall. The project was a complete success.

After that I served several more years in the Marine Corps until I retired. I was immediately hired by a company supporting military budget analyses at three times the salary I was making at a Lt Col in the Marines. And I was the Division Manager for 33 programmers and analysts. All because of those three hard years automating the officer assignment system. I held that job for 7 years. I was then hired by another company to develop new technologies for special operations forces, which I held for a few years.

But here is the point to my story. While in that job, a program manager from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) visited the company as they were interested in our work. The program manager asked if I'd like to become an independent consultant for his program at DARPA and I took that opportunity. I was paid by the hour but I made between $120,000 and $190,000 a year working out of my tiny home office traveling to wherever the program manager wanted me to go and doing whatever he needed me to do. I wrote technical papers, did technical training for the military, demonstrated new technologies, was the technical support for new technologies on military exercises, worked closely with the DARPA development teams, and I travel a lot. I lost count of the times I flew across the US, was on business for the Navy in Hawaii 25 times, and I traveled around the world several times over supporting military training and exercises.

Had it not been for that assignment at Headquarters Marine Corps, when I retired I would have been little more than an old war horse bagging groceries somewhere.

As Forrest Gump said, "Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you are going to get."

I was lucky. As an independent consultant, I never had to solicit new business. I always had clients and it was just by word of mouth about the quality of my support.

That is not typical. Most people who work for themselves have to find new clients by advertising, cold calls, or submitting proposals. I didn't. All of my clients came to me and I could often pick and chose what programs I wanted to support.

The Marine Corps was one heck of an experience and wouldn't trade it for anything. I learned a lot working for two companies. But the most satisfying job I had was working for myself. I'd still be doing it but the travel requirements were too much and after 50 years of working, I figured I'd earned some time for myself.

Just some of my insights and luck. I doubt it will be helpful, but it's how I wandered through life and enjoyed it. I think I just liked doing so many different things both in my jobs and in my free time. I'd do it all again if I could.
